title: BQP versus BPP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Prove or disprove that bounded-error polynomial-time quantum computation can solve a decision problem that no bounded-error polynomial-time classical algorithm can solve, without an oracle.
status: Open since the formulation of quantum complexity theory. Oracle separations and candidate applications do not establish the unrelativized separation.
why: Establishes whether quantum computers fundamentally enlarge efficient computation.
key_works: John Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.

title: NP-complete problems in BQP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether NP is contained in BQP; equivalently, whether a quantum computer can solve an NP-complete decision problem in polynomial time.
status: Open. Grover-type improvements concern search complexity and do not give polynomial-time algorithms for unrestricted NP-complete problems.
why: Determines whether quantum computing can efficiently solve general combinatorial search rather than selected structured problems.
key_works: Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.

title: The unrelativized relationship between BQP and PH
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether BQP is contained in the polynomial hierarchy, whether PH is contained in BQP, or whether they are incomparable.
status: Oracle evidence separates quantum computation from PH, but it does not resolve these containments for ordinary computation.
why: Locates quantum computation relative to classical alternation and approximate counting.
key_works: Scott Aaronson (2010), *BQP and the polynomial hierarchy*, DOI:10.1145/1806689.1806711; Ran Raz and Avishay Tal (2019), *Oracle separation of BQP and PH*, DOI:10.1145/3313276.3316315.

title: QMA versus QCMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Prove or disprove that polynomial-size quantum witnesses provide more verification power than polynomial-size classical witnesses for a quantum verifier.
status: The unrelativized question remains open. Classical-oracle separations were obtained in 2026; the older “find a classical-oracle separation” formulation is therefore not the remaining problem.
why: Identifies whether useful evidence can be intrinsically quantum.
key_works: John Bostanci, Jonas Haferkamp, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Separating QMA from QCMA with a Classical Oracle*, STOC 2026.

title: Perfect completeness for QMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether QMA equals QMA₁ for a specified standard finite gate set: can every valid instance have a witness accepted with certainty?
status: Open. Recent amplification results improve completeness dramatically but also establish black-box limitations; arbitrarily small error is not perfect completeness.
why: Clarifies the role of unavoidable verification error in quantum proofs.
key_works: Scott Aaronson, Phillip Harris, and Freek Witteveen (2025; revised 2026), *Limits to black-box amplification in QMA*, arXiv:2509.21131.

title: The power of unentangled quantum witnesses
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether QMA(2), with two unentangled witnesses, equals QMA or is strictly more powerful.
status: The ordinary complexity-class question remains open. A September 2026 preprint establishes a quantum-oracle separation and resolves the associated no-disentanglers conjecture, not the unrelativized equality.
why: Determines how much computational power comes from a promise about independence.
key_works: John Bostanci et al. (2026), *A quantum oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA*, arXiv:2609.02865.

title: Quantum Valiant–Vazirani isolation
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Construct a randomized polynomial-time reduction from general QMA verification to verification with a unique accepting quantum witness, with suitable completeness and soundness promises.
status: Open for unrestricted QMA. Classical and restricted quantum analogues do not provide a general quantum witness-isolation theorem.
why: Would transfer uniqueness-based algorithms and hardness arguments into quantum complexity.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Michael Ben-Or, Fernando Brandão, and Or Sattath (2008), *The Pursuit of Uniqueness: Extending Valiant-Vazirani Theorem to the Probabilistic and Quantum Settings*, arXiv:0810.4840.

title: Error reduction for StoqMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether StoqMA verification admits general efficient error reduction while preserving its restricted computational structure.
status: Open since StoqMA’s introduction. Aharonov–Grilo–Liu show that suitable error reduction would imply StoqMA = MA.
why: Tests whether stoquastic verification genuinely exceeds classical randomized verification.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Alex B. Grilo, and Yupan Liu (2020/2025), *StoqMA vs. MA: the power of error reduction*, arXiv:2010.02835; DOI:10.22331/q-2025-09-11-1853.

title: The quantum PCP conjecture
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Prove or disprove QMA-hardness of approximating the ground-state energy density of bounded-locality, bounded-degree Hamiltonians to a constant additive accuracy.
status: Open. Good quantum codes, NLTS constructions, and recent locally testable-code claims do not themselves establish quantum PCP.
why: Determines whether extensive quantum entanglement remains computationally essential at nonzero energy density.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Itai Arad, and Thomas Vidick (2013), *The Quantum PCP Conjecture*, arXiv:1309.7495; Sevag Gharibian (2026), *Hardness of Approximation for Ground State Problems*.

title: Spectral gap amplification without destroying locality
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Amplify a local Hamiltonian’s promise gap to a constant fraction of its extensive energy scale while preserving efficient reductions, bounded locality, and the relevant low-energy structure.
status: Open in the form needed for quantum PCP. October 2026 work addresses combinatorial soundness amplification, which is not a general spectral amplification theorem.
why: Supplies a potential missing component of a quantum PCP proof.
key_works: Mitali Bafna, Quynh T. Nguyen, and Tina Zhang (2026), *Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness*, arXiv:2610.04952.

title: General commuting local Hamiltonians in NP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether every bounded-locality commuting local Hamiltonian problem has polynomial-size classical certificates for its low-energy promise.
status: Open generally. Bostanci–Hwang’s 2026 results extend NP containment to important rank-one cases beyond two dimensions, but not arbitrary commuting interactions.
why: Separates computational difficulty caused by noncommutativity from difficulty caused by entanglement.
key_works: John Bostanci and Yeongwoo Hwang (2026), *Commuting Local Hamiltonians Beyond 2D*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.25.

title: No low-energy samplable states
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Construct local Hamiltonian families for which every sufficiently low-energy state escapes the relevant efficient classical sampling-description class, as formalized by the NLSS conjecture.
status: Open beyond restricted state families. Exclusions of Clifford, almost-Clifford, and fermionic Gaussian low-energy states are partial results, not the full claim.
why: Strengthens the evidence that low-energy quantum matter cannot be represented by tractable classical models.
key_works: Kartik Anand (2025), *Constructing Fermionic Hamiltonians with Non-Gaussianic low-energy states*, arXiv:2502.15368.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum separation for total functions
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Determine the optimal exponent relating randomized query complexity \(R(f)\) and bounded-error quantum query complexity \(Q(f)\) for total Boolean functions.
status: The general gap between known large separations and upper bounds remains unresolved; the 2025 survey records cubic-type separations versus a quartic general upper bound.
why: Measures quantum speedup without hiding difficulty in a promise.
key_works: Yassine Hamoudi (2025), *A Brief Introduction to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2508.08852; Aaronson (2021), *Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2109.06917.

title: Optimal quantum complexity of k-distinctness
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Obtain matching quantum query upper and lower bounds for detecting a value occurring at least \(k\) times, for each fixed \(k\geq3\), and understand growing \(k\).
status: Open beyond element distinctness. Learning graphs and multidimensional quantum walks improve algorithms, but do not settle the complete exponent landscape.
why: Tests the limits of quantum walks and collision-finding techniques.
key_works: Stacey Jeffery and Sebastian Zur (2022), *Multidimensional Quantum Walks, with Application to k-Distinctness*, arXiv:2208.13492.

title: Tight quantum triangle-finding bounds
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of triangle detection in the adjacency-matrix model, including tight dependence on graph sparsity.
status: Open. Improved and derandomized algorithms do not close the upper–lower-bound gap.
why: Provides a central test case for quantum graph algorithms beyond unstructured search.
key_works: Guanzhong Li and Lvzhou Li (2023), *Derandomization of quantum algorithm for triangle finding*, arXiv:2309.13268; François Le Gall and Shogo Nakajima (2015), *Quantum Algorithm for Triangle Finding in Sparse Graphs*, arXiv:1507.06878.

title: Polynomial-time dihedral hidden subgroup algorithms
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Find a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup or dihedral coset problem, or prove meaningful limitations for broad algorithmic models.
status: Open. A claimed August 2026 solution was explicitly refuted; that algorithm cannot recover even the required secret bit with non-negligible advantage.
why: Would substantially change the quantum algorithmic landscape for lattice-related problems.
key_works: Andrew Childs and Wim van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380; Aparna Gupte, Seyoon Ragavan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP*, ePrint:2026/1693.

title: Efficient nonabelian hidden subgroup algorithms for graph isomorphism
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Develop an efficient quantum algorithm for the symmetric-group hidden subgroup instances arising from graph isomorphism, overcoming measurement and postprocessing barriers.
status: Open. Abelian Fourier sampling and several nonabelian special cases do not resolve these instances.
why: Would extend quantum algebraic speedups beyond the structures used by factoring and discrete logarithms.
key_works: Childs and van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380; DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.82.1.

title: Tight complexity under restricted unitary access
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Classify natural search, estimation, and learning tasks when access permits only \(U\), rather than freely supplying \(U^\dagger\), controlled-\(U\), transpose, and conjugate operations.
status: Newly sharpened frontier. Recent separations show that familiar oracle conventions can hide essential computational resources; a complete task-by-task classification is absent.
why: Makes algorithmic speedups meaningful for experimentally supplied quantum processes.
key_works: Ewin Tang, John Wright, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Quantum oracles, weak and strong*; Blake Holman, Ronak Ramachandran, and Justin Yirka (2025), *Quantum Search with In-Place Queries*.

title: Computational complexity of Uhlmann transformations
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Characterize when a unitary mapping between compatible purifications can be synthesized efficiently, especially for succinctly specified mixed states without privileged purification access.
status: Structural completeness and equivalence results exist; efficient synthesis for important promised families remains unresolved.
why: Connects quantum state conversion, cryptography, and recovery of encoded information.
key_works: John Bostanci, Yuval Efron, Tony Metger, Alexander Poremba, Luowen Qian, and Henry Yuen (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.

title: Generic accuracy amplification for state and unitary synthesis
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Determine which state-generation and unitary-synthesis complexity classes permit exponentially improved accuracy with only polynomial overhead.
status: Open in general. Decision-problem amplification does not automatically amplify the fidelity of an output state or implemented transformation.
why: Prevents small synthesis errors from becoming an unaccounted resource in composed quantum algorithms.
key_works: Bostanci et al. (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.

title: Permanent-of-Gaussians conjecture
open: Establish the appropriate average-case hardness of approximating permanents of independent complex Gaussian matrices, with the precision and success probability needed for approximate boson-sampling hardness.
status: Open since the original boson-sampling proposal. Worst-case permanent hardness is insufficient.
why: Supplies a missing complexity assumption behind robust linear-optical sampling advantage.
key_works: Scott Aaronson and Alex Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245; DOI:10.1145/1993636.1993682.

title: Permanent anticoncentration
open: Prove sufficiently strong lower-tail bounds for the permanent of a Gaussian matrix, at its natural \(\sqrt{n!}\) scale, to support approximate-sampling reductions.
status: Open in the required general form. This is distinct from proving that permanent estimation is computationally hard.
why: Converts additive probability-estimation information into useful multiplicative information.
key_works: Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245.

title: Average-case hafnian hardness for Gaussian boson sampling
open: Establish the average-case hardness and anticoncentration statements needed for the experimentally relevant Gaussian-boson-sampling distributions, including their structured matrix ensembles.
status: Open in robust approximate-sampling formulations. Exact hafnian hardness alone does not settle noisy experimental distributions.
why: Places Gaussian photonic advantage on firmer complexity foundations.
key_works: Craig S. Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.170501; Daniel Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*.

title: Robust average-case hardness of random-circuit sampling
open: Prove sampling hardness under experimentally meaningful constant total-variation error using defensible average-case assumptions, rather than only exact or extremely high-precision probability estimation.
status: Open at the strongest useful noise-robust level. Existing worst-to-average-case reductions do not automatically deliver that statement.
why: Distinguishes a mathematical hardness theorem from an extrapolation to noisy devices.
key_works: Adam Bouland, Bill Fefferman, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Umesh Vazirani (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402.

title: Sharp loss and distinguishability boundaries in photonic sampling
open: Determine tight efficiently-simulable versus plausibly-hard regimes as photon survival, distinguishability, squeezing, and mode count scale together.
status: Numerous sufficient simulation and hardness regimes exist, but their boundaries do not form a complete phase diagram.
why: Identifies which component improvements actually preserve computational hardness.
key_works: Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.22331/q-2022-11-28-863; Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*.

title: Efficient certification of hard sampling distributions
open: Certify closeness to a specified hard quantum distribution using feasible classical computation and samples, under explicit restrictions strong enough to make certification possible but weak enough to exclude realistic spoofers.
status: Open as a general practical certification problem; efficient tests usually certify selected statistics, assumptions, or restricted alternatives.
why: A sampler’s apparent complexity is not evidence that it sampled the intended distribution.
key_works: Bouland et al. (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402; Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*.

title: Low-temperature mixing times of quantum Gibbs samplers
open: Prove useful mixing-time bounds for explicit noncommuting many-body Hamiltonians at temperatures where correlations and metastability make classical sampling difficult.
status: Efficiently implementable exact-detailed-balance generators exist; their existence does not imply rapid mixing for arbitrary low-temperature systems.
why: State preparation can dominate the cost of otherwise efficient simulation.
key_works: Chi-Fang Chen, Michael J. Kastoryano, and András Gilyén (2023; revised 2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207.

title: End-to-end Gibbs-sampling advantage for frustrated magnets
open: Demonstrate a total-cost quantum advantage for preparing and measuring thermal states of a specified frustrated magnet, including mixing, initialization, error correction, and observable estimation.
status: An application-level target, not a consequence of having an efficient Lindbladian implementation.
why: Could resolve finite-temperature regimes inaccessible to reliable classical sampling.
key_works: Chen, Kastoryano, and Gilyén (2023/2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207.

title: Certifiable initial overlap for phase estimation
open: Efficiently certify a useful lower bound on a prepared state’s overlap with the desired eigenstate, without already solving the hard spectral problem.
status: System-specific heuristics and bounds exist; a broadly useful certification procedure for strongly correlated chemistry remains missing.
why: Resource estimates can become misleading when they assume an unverified state-preparation success probability.
key_works: Joonho Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199.

title: Reliable ground-state preparation for strongly correlated instances
open: Develop preparation methods with demonstrated scaling guarantees or reproducible success across a specified class of strongly correlated molecules or materials, rather than isolated favorable instances.
status: Adiabatic, variational, filtering, and phase-estimation approaches offer partial solutions; no unrestricted efficient algorithm is expected.
why: Converts Hamiltonian-simulation capability into dependable scientific calculations.
key_works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Markus Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*.

title: Sharp state- and observable-dependent Trotter error bounds
open: Obtain efficiently evaluable error bounds that exploit the actual initial state and measured observable, and that remain predictive at useful simulation times.
status: General commutator-based product-formula bounds are established; tight instance-specific certificates remain substantially less developed.
why: Could remove large safety margins without silently sacrificing accuracy.
key_works: Andrew Childs, Yuan Su, Minh C. Tran, Nathan Wiebe, and Shuchen Zhu (2021), *A Theory of Trotter Error*, arXiv:1912.08854; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.11.011020.

title: Long-time local-observable simulation beyond generic light cones
open: Exploit hydrodynamic, mixing, or other verifiable physical promises to estimate local observables at long times with costs substantially below generic full-state simulation.
status: Nearly optimal general lattice-evolution algorithms exist; favorable long-time reductions require additional promises and are not generic fast-forwarding.
why: Transport and equilibration often matter more than reconstructing an entire wavefunction.
key_works: Jeongwan Haah, Matthew Hastings, Robin Kothari, and Guang Hao Low (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*, arXiv:1801.03922.

title: Certified truncation of unbounded bosonic and gauge degrees of freedom
open: Derive practical, state-dependent truncation bounds for interacting bosonic and gauge-field simulations, including particle production and long-time dynamics.
status: Rigorous bounds exist for selected models and regimes; universal small cutoffs cannot be assumed.
why: Determines whether a finite qubit encoding accurately represents an infinite-dimensional physical system.
key_works: Stephen Jordan, Keith Lee, and John Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633; Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.

title: Useful fault-tolerant simulation of open many-body systems
open: Establish a practical advantage for a specified driven-dissipative many-body model after accounting for Lindbladian implementation, steady-state mixing, measurement, and fault tolerance.
status: Polynomial simulation theorems are established; they do not establish a favorable scientific crossover.
why: Opens calculations of dissipative phases, transport, and nonequilibrium steady states.
key_works: Martin Kliesch, Thomas Barthel, Christian Gogolin, Michael Kastoryano, and Jens Eisert (2011), *A dissipative quantum Church-Turing theorem*, arXiv:1105.3986.

title: Certified FeMoco spin-state and energy ordering
open: Compute chemically decisive FeMoco energy differences with a complete uncertainty budget covering the electronic Hamiltonian, active space, state preparation, and quantum numerical error.
status: Resource-estimation studies establish plausible computational routes, not a certified solution of the relevant chemical ordering.
why: Tests quantum computing on a scientifically consequential strongly correlated system.
key_works: Markus Reiher, Nathan Wiebe, Krysta Svore, Dave Wecker, and Matthias Troyer (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590.

title: Quantum-assisted nitrogenase reaction kinetics
open: Go beyond an isolated electronic-energy calculation to a validated nitrogen-fixation reaction pathway, including competing intermediates, environmental effects, and rate-determining steps.
status: A downstream application gap beyond FeMoco resource estimates; accurate energies alone do not determine a complete catalytic mechanism.
why: Connects quantum calculations to catalyst understanding rather than benchmark energies.
key_works: Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590; Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.

title: Validated quantum advantage in industrial catalysis
open: Demonstrate that a quantum calculation changes a catalyst-selection or process-design decision more accurately or cheaply than the strongest available classical workflow.
status: Detailed catalytic case studies and resource estimates exist; decision-level advantage requires preparation, uncertainty, and experimental validation together.
why: Establishes an economically meaningful chemistry use case.
key_works: Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.

title: Coupled electronic–nuclear nonadiabatic dynamics
open: Simulate a chemically important nonadiabatic process with controlled errors in electronic correlation, nuclear motion, conical-intersection behavior, and measured reaction observables.
status: Electronic-structure algorithms are more mature than complete coupled-dynamics workflows; favorable scaling must include initial-state preparation and readout.
why: Addresses photochemistry and reaction dynamics that static energies cannot capture.
key_works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*.

title: Controlled low-temperature phase diagram of the doped Hubbard model
open: Resolve specified competing phases and correlations of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model with thermodynamic-limit and low-temperature error control.
status: Extensive classical benchmarks constrain portions of the diagram; quantum simulation must still demonstrate controlled answers in the disputed regimes.
why: Tests proposed microscopic explanations of correlated-electron phenomena.
key_works: J. P. F. LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model: Benchmarks and Results from a Wide Range of Numerical Algorithms*, arXiv:1505.02290.

title: Real-frequency response of strongly correlated materials
open: Obtain controlled spectral functions and transport responses in regimes where analytic continuation and classical real-time entanglement growth are major obstacles.
status: Ground-state and imaginary-time benchmarks are substantial; reliable long-time, real-frequency results remain model- and regime-dependent.
why: Produces quantities directly comparable with spectroscopy and transport experiments.
key_works: LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model*, arXiv:1505.02290; Haah et al. (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*.

title: Finite-density QCD with controlled state preparation
open: Prepare and measure finite-baryon-density gauge-theory states with demonstrated resource scaling, gauge fidelity, and continuum extrapolation.
status: Quantum-simulation proposals address the classical sign problem conceptually, but avoiding that problem does not automatically make preparation efficient.
why: Could access dense strongly interacting matter beyond standard Monte Carlo methods.
key_works: Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.

title: Real-time nonabelian gauge dynamics near the continuum
open: Compute a nontrivial real-time SU(3) observable with controlled errors from lattice spacing, finite volume, electric-field truncation, state preparation, and quantum execution.
status: Lower-dimensional and truncated demonstrations are context, not a complete continuum-QCD calculation.
why: Could address scattering, hadronization, and nonequilibrium strong-interaction physics.
key_works: Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633.

title: Quantum preconditioners with honest implementation cost
open: Construct preconditioners that improve a quantum linear-system solver’s total gate complexity after including their construction, block encoding, application, and data-access costs.
status: General matrix-transformation machinery is established; a classical preconditioner is not automatically an efficient quantum oracle.
why: Condition-number dependence can erase nominal linear-algebra speedups.
key_works: András Gilyén, Yuan Su, Guang Hao Low, and Nathan Wiebe (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for quantum matrix arithmetics*, arXiv:1806.01838.

title: Output-aware quantum linear algebra
open: Classify applications where the desired classical output can be extracted cheaply enough that quantum state preparation and linear-system solving yield an end-to-end advantage.
status: Preparing a solution state is well understood under suitable access assumptions; recovering a full classical solution generally changes the complexity.
why: Prevents state-output algorithms from being misrepresented as fast replacements for arbitrary classical solvers.
key_works: Gilyén et al. (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond*, arXiv:1806.01838.

title: Nonlinear differential equations beyond strong dissipativity
open: Extend efficient quantum nonlinear-ODE methods to useful regimes outside their favorable dissipation and nonlinearity assumptions, or prove sharp limitations.
status: Carleman-based algorithms establish advantages in restricted dissipative regimes; unrestricted nonlinear evolution cannot inherit those guarantees.
why: Determines applicability to realistic nonlinear dynamics rather than carefully conditioned examples.
key_works: Jin-Peng Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185.

title: Stiff nonlinear dynamics with certified quantum truncation
open: Develop adaptive truncation and conditioning strategies for stiff nonlinear equations that preserve an advantage after solution growth, normalization, and output estimation are included.
status: Existing nonlinear quantum algorithms expose these dependencies but do not solve general stiffness and adaptive-error control.
why: Stiffness is common in chemistry, plasma physics, and multiscale engineering.
key_works: Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185.

title: Practical amplitude-estimation advantage for Monte Carlo
open: Demonstrate a full-workflow advantage on a consequential expectation-estimation problem, including reversible sampling, payoff evaluation, fault tolerance, and statistical confidence.
status: Quadratic query improvements are established; their wall-clock and energy advantages are not automatic.
why: Monte Carlo is ubiquitous, but expensive coherent oracles can consume the speedup.
key_works: Ashley Montanaro (2015), *Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods*, arXiv:1504.06987; Ryan Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Useful quantum backtracking on structured search
open: Identify and demonstrate structured constraint families where quantum backtracking beats strong classical heuristics after reversible constraint checking and search-tree construction are charged.
status: Quantum speedups in tree size are established; practical advantage depends on the actual tree and implementation overhead.
why: Connects quantum search to real combinatorial workloads.
key_works: Ashley Montanaro (2015/2016), *Quantum walk speedup of backtracking algorithms*, arXiv:1509.02374.

title: Fixed-angle QAOA conjectures
open: Prove or refute the fixed-angle performance conjectures for QAOA on regular MaxCut graph families, with explicit depth and graph-size dependence.
status: Open conjectural territory beyond analytically solved shallow cases and numerical evidence.
why: Would replace expensive instance-by-instance parameter searches with justified reusable schedules.
key_works: Jonathan Wurtz and Danylo Lykov (2021), *Fixed-angle conjectures for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on regular MaxCut graphs*, Physical Review A 104, 052419.

title: QAOA beyond overlap-gap barriers
open: Identify problem structure, depth scaling, or algorithmic modifications that yield provable useful approximation improvements outside known overlap-gap obstructions.
status: Low-depth barriers and landscape results rule out several naive routes; exceeding them is not established by successful small-instance optimization.
why: Separates meaningful optimization progress from parameter-fitting demonstrations.
key_works: Mark Xin Hong Goh (2026), *The overlap gap property and its implication for the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm*, doctoral thesis.

title: Trainable, expressive, non-dequantizable variational models
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Exhibit a useful model family that is efficiently trainable, sufficiently expressive for its task, and not efficiently replaceable by a comparably informed classical model.
status: These properties are individually studied; satisfying all three with convincing scaling evidence remains a central gap.
why: Avoids trading away quantum advantage to eliminate barren plateaus.
key_works: Martin Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2405.00781; DOI:10.1038/s42254-025-00813-9.

title: Noise-resilient trainability at useful circuit depth
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Maintain informative gradients or an alternative efficient training signal at depths needed for a target advantage, under measured noise and finite sampling budgets.
status: Noise-free initialization fixes do not solve noise-induced loss of training signal.
why: Training can fail before the underlying model loses formal expressive power.
key_works: Jarrod McClean et al. (2018), *Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*.

title: Adaptive generalization from quantum experimental data
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Derive sharp generalization and sample-complexity guarantees when an experimental quantum learner adaptively chooses measurements, reuses learned representations, and faces distribution shift.
status: Quantum learning advantages exist for selected data models; they do not provide a universal adaptive generalization theory.
why: Makes learned scientific predictions trustworthy outside the training experiment.
key_works: Hsin-Yuan Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778; DOI:10.1126/science.abn7293.

title: Quantum kernel advantage under matched data access
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Establish useful learning advantages while charging quantum and classical methods consistently for data loading, sampling access, preprocessing, and model selection.
status: Dequantization results show that apparently quantum speedups can depend on unequal access assumptions.
why: Distinguishes a computational advantage from an input-model advantage.
key_works: Ewin Tang (2019), *A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems*, arXiv:1807.04271; M. Cerezo et al. (2021), *Variational Quantum Algorithms*.

title: Practical quantum processing of massive classical streams
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Realize a classical-data streaming task with a measured total-resource advantage, including sketch construction, coherent processing, repeated inference, and model output.
status: Zhao et al.’s 2026 work establishes important model-specific exponential advantages; practical wall-clock advantage is a separate target.
why: Could make quantum learning relevant without requiring that all input data originate in a quantum experiment.
key_works: Haimeng Zhao et al. (2026), *Exponential quantum advantage in processing massive classical data*.

title: Quantum-data learning advantage after storage and error correction
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Demonstrate that a quantum learner’s sample advantage survives the cost of preserving, routing, and jointly processing quantum training data.
status: Exponential measurement advantages are established for selected tasks; sample count alone does not account for the complete experimental system.
why: Determines whether quantum memory is economically justified as part of a learning pipeline.
key_works: Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778.

title: Valid confidence intervals for adaptive classical shadows
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Produce tight confidence guarantees when observables are selected after inspecting shadow data, with realistic measurement errors and repeated adaptive queries.
status: Standard shadow guarantees cover important predetermined-observable settings; unrestricted adaptive reuse needs additional control.
why: Prevents exploratory quantum experiments from reporting selection-biased discoveries.
key_works: Hsin-Yuan Huang, Richard Kueng, and John Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: Efficient measurement of difficult many-body observables
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Identify experimentally implementable measurement ensembles with manageable sample complexity for physically important nonlocal observables whose standard shadow norms are large.
status: Classical shadows do not make every observable efficiently estimable; favorable measurement design remains task-specific.
why: Measurement cost can dominate otherwise efficient state preparation.
key_works: Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: SIC measurements in every finite dimension
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Prove that a symmetric informationally complete POVM exists in every finite Hilbert-space dimension, or identify a counterexample dimension.
status: Open. Exact and numerical constructions in many dimensions do not establish the universal statement.
why: Would provide a uniform optimal geometric structure for informationally complete quantum measurements.
key_works: Joseph Renes et al. (2004), *Symmetric informationally complete quantum measurements*; Paweł Horodecki, Łukasz Rudnicki, and Karol Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.

title: Four mutually unbiased bases in dimension six
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Construct four mutually unbiased orthonormal bases of \(\mathbb C^6\), or prove that no such quartet exists.
status: Open. Three are available; the prime-power construction of complete sets does not settle dimension six.
why: Probes the arithmetic obstruction behind optimal complementary measurements.
key_works: Horodecki, Rudnicki, and Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.

title: Negative-partial-transpose bound entanglement
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Establish whether a negative-partial-transpose state can remain undistillable for every finite number of copies.
status: Open. A July 2026 preprint solves the two-copy Werner-state problem, but explicitly leaves the arbitrary-copy endpoint problem unresolved.
why: Determines whether detectable entanglement can remain permanently unusable for singlet distillation.
key_works: Kishor Bharti, Rishikesh Gajjala, and Tobias Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states: sharp partial-trace inequalities and finite-copy extensions*, arXiv:2607.24479.

title: Exact distillation rates for Werner-state families
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Determine optimal asymptotic singlet-distillation rates across the distillable region of specified Werner-state families, including the benefit of collective processing.
status: Distillability and rate are different questions. Recent finite-copy threshold results do not determine the complete rate function.
why: Quantifies usable entanglement rather than merely deciding whether some can be extracted.
key_works: Bharti, Gajjala, and Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states*, arXiv:2607.24479.

title: Exact quantum capacity of the depolarizing channel
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Determine the quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel throughout its nontrivial parameter range, including whether and where regularization is essential.
status: Open. Improved upper bounds, coding constructions, and strong-converse results do not yield the exact capacity curve.
why: Provides a fundamental benchmark for transmitting quantum information through symmetric noise.
key_works: Tulja Varun Kondra et al. (2026), *Sharp Quantum Capacity Thresholds: Exponential Strong Converses for Degradable and Antidegradable Channels*, arXiv:2608.01308; Zhiwei Song et al. (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*.

title: Exact two-way capacity of thermal-loss channels
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Close the gap between achievable rates and upper bounds for entanglement or secret-key generation through thermal-loss bosonic channels with two-way classical communication.
status: Exact pure-loss benchmarks are established; thermal noise leaves important capacity gaps.
why: Determines the ultimate value of quantum repeaters and transducers in realistic optical links.
key_works: Stefano Pirandola, Riccardo Laurenza, Carlo Ottaviani, and Leonardo Banchi (2017), *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.

title: Exact reliability and strong-converse exponents
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Determine optimal error-decay and success-decay exponents as functions of rate for important quantum channels, rather than merely showing exponential decay.
status: A September 2026 preprint claims general exponential strong converses for finite-dimensional memoryless capacities; exact exponent functions remain a finer question.
why: Converts asymptotic capacities into quantitative finite-blocklength guidance.
key_works: Salman Beigi and Marco Tomamichel (2026), *Strong Converses for Quantum Channel Capacities from Blowing-Up Lemmata*, arXiv:2609.11771.

title: Exact output majorization for depolarizing channels
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Prove or refute the exact output-majorization conjecture for tensor powers of depolarizing channels, beyond approximate majorization guarantees.
status: Open. September 2026 work proves approximate majorization and sharp higher-order consequences without resolving the exact conjecture.
why: Could tightly constrain the benefit of entangled inputs in channel coding.
key_works: Zhiwei Song, Xin Wang, Marco Tomamichel, and Kun Fang (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*, arXiv:2609.37240.

title: Publicly verifiable quantum computation from weaker assumptions
open: Obtain publicly verifiable classical verification of general quantum computations from substantially weaker or better-understood assumptions than quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.
status: New September 2026 constructions provide public verification under strong assumptions; existence under those assumptions is not the remaining gap.
why: Reduces the cryptographic assumptions behind auditable quantum cloud results.
key_works: Alexandru Gheorghiu, Aparna Gupte, Vojtěch Havlíček, and Yunchao Liu (2026), *Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfuscation*, arXiv:2609.40289.

title: Practical classical verification with realistic constants
open: Implement classical verification of a useful quantum workload with measured prover, verifier, communication, and fault-tolerance costs that preserve the workload’s advantage.
status: Quasilinear asymptotic resource constructions were reported in September 2026; practical constants and complete systems remain separate questions.
why: Makes verification usable rather than merely polynomial.
key_works: Finn Holler and Anand Natarajan (2026), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computation with Quasilinear Resources, from Compiled Nonlocal Games*, arXiv:2609.38060; Urmila Mahadev (2018), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computations*, arXiv:1804.01082.

title: Low-overhead fault-tolerant blind delegation
open: Demonstrate useful delegated computation that simultaneously preserves input and program privacy, detects cheating, and tolerates physical noise at competitive total overhead.
status: Universal blind computation and theoretical fault-tolerant extensions already exist; the unresolved target is integrated useful-scale performance.
why: Enables confidential use of remote quantum hardware.
key_works: Anne Broadbent, Joseph Fitzsimons, and Elham Kashefi (2009), *Universal blind quantum computation*, arXiv:0807.4154; DOI:10.1109/FOCS.2009.36.

title: Practical quantum fully homomorphic encryption
open: Reduce and experimentally validate the complete overhead of homomorphically evaluating useful quantum circuits, including key management, non-Clifford evaluation, noise, and decryption.
status: Cryptographic constructions exist; compactness and polynomial complexity do not establish practical deployment.
why: Permits computation on encrypted quantum data without revealing it to the server.
key_works: Urmila Mahadev (2017; revised 2023), *Classical Homomorphic Encryption for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1708.02130.

title: Noise-tolerant unclonable credentials
open: Construct and demonstrate unclonable signing tokens or credentials whose security survives explicit storage noise, recovery operations, repeated verification, and device imperfections.
status: Memory-efficient cryptographic constructions advanced in 2026; asymptotically small quantum keys are not yet a complete noisy-device solution.
why: Turns no-cloning-based cryptography into usable persistent credentials.
key_works: Andrew Huang, Omri Shmueli, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Unclonable Cryptography in Linear Quantum Memory*, CRYPTO 2026.

title: High-throughput cryptographically certified randomness
open: Produce a positive, competitive net rate of certified random bits after accounting for cryptographic challenges, seed use, finite statistics, hardware noise, and verification.
status: Single-device cryptographic certification protocols are established; useful operating rates and complete security accounting remain engineering targets.
why: Provides verifiable randomness without trusting a device’s internal implementation.
key_works: Zvika Brakerski et al. (2018), *A Cryptographic Test of Quantumness and Certifiable Randomness from a Single Quantum Device*, arXiv:1804.00640.

title: Minimum realistic resources for RSA-2048 factoring
open: Determine the best defensible physical-qubit, runtime, energy, and reliability tradeoff for factoring RSA-2048 under explicitly measured hardware assumptions.
status: Estimates continue to improve. Gidney’s 2025 sub-million-noisy-qubit proposal is a resource analysis, not an experimental factorization.
why: Grounds cryptographic migration and hardware planning in auditable costs.
key_works: Craig Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917.

title: Honest quantum resource models for lattice cryptanalysis
open: Produce reproducible end-to-end resource estimates for leading quantum lattice attacks, including coherent memory, reversible sieving, classical preprocessing, and error correction.
status: Algorithmic proposals and lower-level costs remain easy to conflate; refuted hidden-subgroup shortcuts illustrate the need for independently checked analyses.
why: Separates meaningful quantum threats from unsupported oracle-cost assumptions.
key_works: Gupte, Ragavan, and Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP*, ePrint:2026/1693; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Finite-size qLDPC computation advantage
open: Demonstrate a complete finite-size computation where a quantum LDPC architecture uses fewer total physical resources than a well-optimized surface-code implementation at the same failure probability.
status: Low-overhead memory designs and simulations are strong partial results; memory savings do not automatically survive universal gates and routing.
why: Tests whether high-rate codes reduce the cost of actual computation.
key_works: Sergey Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07107-7.

title: Circuit-level single-shot decoding in practical qLDPC devices
open: Integrate single-shot decoding with realistic syndrome circuits, measurement correlations, leakage, and bounded classical latency while preserving a finite-size advantage.
status: Single-shot decoding of good quantum LDPC codes is established theoretically; its generic existence should not be relisted as open.
why: Could reduce repeated-measurement time and simplify fault-tolerant control.
key_works: Shouzhen Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*, arXiv:2306.12470; DOI:10.1007/s00220-024-04951-6.

title: Practical constants for good quantum locally testable codes
open: Obtain explicit, usable finite-size tradeoffs among rate, distance, check weight, soundness, and construction complexity for good quantum locally testable codes.
status: A September 2026 preprint claims asymptotically good qubit QLTCs. The remaining target here is practical parameters, not their bare asymptotic existence.
why: Determines whether local testability can materially improve real architectures.
key_works: William Gay and Fernando Granha Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780.

title: Efficient decoding matched to good QLTC constructions
open: Supply explicit decoders and provable noise tolerances for new good QLTC constructions, with computational costs compatible with repeated physical error correction.
status: A local tester and a distance theorem are not automatically a practical decoder.
why: Turns an existence construction into an operational code family.
key_works: Gay and Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780; Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*.

title: Lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes
open: Construct explicit bounded-degree, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes satisfying the conditions required by the corresponding QLTC construction.
status: The September 2026 construction identifies these complexes as an unresolved combinatorial input.
why: Offers a distinct structured route to strong quantum code parameters.
key_works: Itay Cohen, Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, and Elad Tzalik (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes*, arXiv:2610.00525.

title: Reed–Solomon product expansion over binary extension fields
open: Prove or refute Conjecture 5.6 of Bafna–Li–Nguyen: constant product expansion for the specified bounded-ratio, pairwise-coprime subgroup evaluation sets of sizes \(2^{m_i}+1\), at rates bounded away from one.
status: Explicitly conjectural in the September 2026 paper; broader unrestricted subgroup variants are false.
why: Supplies structured local codes for quantum locally testable-code constructions.
key_works: Mitali Bafna, Anqi Li, and Quynh T. Nguyen (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Product Expansion*, arXiv:2609.26735, Conjecture 5.6.

title: Practical addressable transversal non-Clifford gates
open: Implement addressable non-Clifford logical gates in finite good-code blocks with measured preparation, decoding, parallelism, and physical-connectivity costs.
status: Good-code constructions supporting addressable and parallelizable transversal gates exist; the practical integrated implementation remains the target.
why: Could reduce reliance on large standalone magic-state factories.
key_works: Z. He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864; Virgile Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*, arXiv:2510.19809.

title: Geometric implementation costs of nonlocal quantum codes
open: Determine tight tradeoffs between qLDPC rate and distance advantages and the physical costs of long-range couplers, shuttling, photonic links, and routing congestion.
status: Abstract sparse connectivity does not imply cheap geometric implementation.
why: Prevents architectural comparisons from treating long-range operations as free.
key_works: Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.

title: Decoding mixed erasure, Pauli, leakage, and coherent noise
open: Develop decoders with explicit guarantees or calibrated uncertainty for simultaneous noise mechanisms rather than separately optimized idealized channels.
status: Erasure-aware and channel-specific methods offer gains; a robust unified treatment remains architecture-dependent.
why: Real devices do not maintain a single stationary textbook noise channel.
key_works: Yue Wu, Shimon Kolkowitz, Shruti Puri, and Jeff Thompson (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540; Matt McEwen et al. (2021), *Removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction*.

title: Decoder robustness outside the training distribution
open: Detect and safely handle noise shifts, rare faults, and unseen correlations without silently producing overconfident logical corrections.
status: Learned decoders achieve strong benchmark accuracy; accuracy on familiar noise is not a guarantee under drift or adversarially selected rare events.
why: Decoder failure can become a hidden logical-error floor.
key_works: Johannes Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08148-8.

title: Bounded-latency decoding without backlog
open: Decode continuously at the physical syndrome rate with bounded tail latency, including difficult bursts, while preserving competitive logical accuracy.
status: High-accuracy decoding and real-time demonstrations exist separately or at limited scales; worst-case sustained throughput remains an architectural constraint.
why: Average decoder speed is insufficient when feedback deadlines are strict.
key_works: Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.

title: Logical-error floors at large distance and long duration
open: Establish whether error suppression continues across larger code distances and much longer runs after including correlated bursts, leakage, calibration changes, and decoder faults.
status: Below-threshold surface-code memories are demonstrated; extrapolation to extremely small failure probabilities requires additional evidence.
why: Large algorithms depend on the tail of the error distribution, not only its typical behavior.
key_works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*, arXiv:2408.13687; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y.

title: Fault tolerance against radiation-induced correlated bursts
open: Determine and experimentally validate architecture-level conditions under which measured radiation-induced error bursts can be detected, contained, and corrected without a persistent logical-error floor.
status: Catastrophic correlated bursts have been observed; shielding or average error reduction alone is not a full fault-tolerance argument.
why: A rare chip-wide event can defeat codes designed around local faults.
key_works: Matt McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219.

title: Leakage-removal protocols without hidden correlated damage
open: Design leakage detection and reset that suppress leakage propagation while keeping reset-induced, measurement-induced, and spectator errors below the logical benefit.
status: Leakage-removal methods are demonstrated; scalable joint optimization with the complete syndrome circuit remains open.
why: Leakage violates the computational-subspace assumptions behind many decoder models.
key_works: Matt McEwen et al. (2021), *Removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction*, arXiv:2102.06131.

title: Long universal logical computations with auditable success
open: Run long computations containing memory, entangling gates, non-Clifford gates, measurement, and feed-forward, with an independently checkable end-to-end failure budget.
status: Below-threshold memory and component demonstrations are partial milestones; they do not establish arbitrary long universal execution.
why: Tests the actual product promised by fault tolerance.
key_works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Actual T-state cultivation under coherent fault propagation
open: Certify complete T-state cultivation, including escape and downstream use, under physical noise rather than relying on a Clifford-simulable surrogate.
status: September 2026 work diagnoses a T-versus-S fault-distance discrepancy and supplies corrective flags; experimental full-protocol certification remains separate.
why: Prevents optimistic magic-state estimates from overlooking coherent logical faults.
key_works: Tim Chan, Armands Strikis, Zhu Sun, and Zhenyu Cai (2026), *Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*, arXiv:2609.17706.

title: Continuous magic-state factories with verified yield
open: Operate a factory continuously while tracking accepted-state fidelity, rejection correlations, drift, downtime, and usable delivery rate to computation.
status: Protocol resource estimates and selected-state demonstrations do not establish long-run production yield.
why: Non-Clifford throughput can set the runtime of a fault-tolerant computer.
key_works: Craig Gidney et al. (2024), *Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates*, arXiv:2409.17595; Chan et al. (2026), *Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*.

title: Tight spacetime overhead of fault tolerance
open: Close asymptotic and finite-size gaps between lower bounds and achievable spacetime overhead under explicitly specified noise and architecture assumptions.
status: Constant qubit overhead has strong constructions. An August 2026 preprint rules out constant total spacetime overhead in its model; the tight achievable tradeoff remains finer.
why: Separates qubit-count savings from total computational cost.
key_works: Matthias Christandl, Omar Fawzi, and Ashutosh Goswami (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*, arXiv:2512.02760; Bharti, Haug, and Andrew Tanggara (2026), arXiv:2608.26272.

title: Low-overhead conversion between heterogeneous logical codes
open: Convert encoded information between memory-efficient and gate-efficient code families with a complete fault-tolerance proof and a net benefit after ancillas, routing, and decoding are counted.
status: Code switching and teleportation primitives exist; useful finite-size combinations are not determined by those primitives alone.
why: A single code need not be best for storage, movement, and non-Clifford computation.
key_works: He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864; Christandl et al. (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*.

title: Joint scheduling of logical routing, factories, and memory
open: Optimize complete fault-tolerant schedules under finite factory rates, stochastic failures, limited connectivity, and logical-memory decay, with certified resource estimates.
status: Component-wise optimization is not generally globally optimal.
why: Congestion and starvation can erase gains predicted by isolated gate counts.
key_works: Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Repair and replacement during logical computation
open: Replace failed qubits, control channels, or modules during an ongoing computation without losing encoded data or invalidating the fault-tolerance assumptions.
status: Reconfiguration and continuous hardware replenishment are emerging capabilities; complete logical service continuity is a stronger target.
why: Long computations must survive component failures, not merely stochastic gate errors.
key_works: Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum random-access memory
open: Build a coherently addressable memory with quantified query fidelity and total hardware, routing, initialization, and correction costs that preserve an application-level advantage.
status: QRAM architectures date to 2007–2008; asymptotic query depth does not establish scalable fault-tolerant feasibility.
why: Many attractive algorithms assume coherent data access that dominates their practical cost.
key_works: Vittorio Giovannetti, Seth Lloyd, and Lorenzo Maccone (2008), *Quantum random access memory*, arXiv:0708.1879.

title: Physical realization of three-dimensional passive self-correction
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Implement a physically credible three-dimensional passive memory and demonstrate increasing quantum lifetime with system size at a fixed nonzero temperature.
status: A May 2026 preprint claims an abstract geometrically local 3D self-correcting stabilizer Hamiltonian. Its laboratory realization is a distinct unresolved problem.
why: Could reduce continuous measurement and feedback requirements.
key_works: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, and Ting-Chun Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.

title: Robustness of self-correction to implementation perturbations
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Establish useful stability bounds for passive self-correcting constructions under imperfect couplings, unwanted interactions, disorder, and realistic bath dynamics.
status: Abstract lifetime theorems do not by themselves certify a fabricated Hamiltonian.
why: Self-correction is useful only if it survives errors in the mechanism meant to provide protection.
key_works: Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.

title: Universal fault tolerance with finite-energy GKP states
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Demonstrate universal logical computation using physically prepared finite-energy GKP states, including realistic envelope effects, gates, recovery, and measurement.
status: GKP encoding and many component protocols are established; ideal infinite-energy codewords are not physical resources.
why: Could provide efficient bosonic error correction with favorable concatenation overhead.
key_works: Daniel Gottesman, Alexei Kitaev, and John Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040.

title: GKP correction optimized for photon loss and physical gates
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Find and validate encodings, recovery maps, and gate schedules jointly optimized for photon loss and finite-energy distortions rather than an ideal displacement-only channel.
status: Noise-model-specific improvements exist; the optimal physical architecture remains unsettled.
why: The convenient effective noise model can differ from the device’s actual dominant error.
key_works: Gottesman, Kitaev, and Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040; V. V. Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*.

title: Fast bias-preserving universal cat-qubit gates
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Implement a useful universal gate set while preserving cat-qubit noise bias sufficiently well that the complete encoded architecture retains its overhead advantage.
status: Long bit-flip lifetimes and concatenated demonstrations are important partial results; gates can introduce the suppressed error channel.
why: A good biased memory is not automatically a good biased computer.
key_works: Ulysse Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*; Harald Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025.

title: Correlated-noise control in concatenated bosonic codes
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Quantify and suppress correlations introduced by shared ancillas, pumps, couplers, and recovery circuits so that concatenation continues to improve logical performance.
status: Hardware-efficient concatenated bosonic correction is demonstrated; scalable independence assumptions require further testing.
why: Concatenation benefits can disappear when a shared physical mechanism produces correlated faults.
key_works: Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025.

title: Autonomous bosonic correction during computation
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Combine autonomous stabilization with a useful gate set, measurement, and reset while demonstrating that the complete process outperforms an unencoded implementation.
status: Autonomous stabilization and beyond-break-even memories are partial milestones; useful computation requires compatible operations.
why: Could reduce fast classical-feedback requirements.
key_works: Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*, arXiv:2211.09116; Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*.

title: Scalable fault-tolerant qudit computation
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Establish when encoding and processing more than two levels per physical system reduces total computational cost after leakage, control selectivity, measurement, and decoder complexity are included.
status: Beyond-break-even qudit correction and high-dimensional control are reported; scalable universal advantage over qubit encodings remains architecture-specific.
why: Higher local dimension may reduce hardware count, but can increase every other control burden.
key_works: Benjamin L. Brock et al. (2025), *Quantum error correction of qudits beyond break-even*; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.

title: Microscopic identification of dominant two-level defects
open: Identify which atomic-scale defects dominate loss in specific fabrication stacks, and causally connect their abundance to qubit relaxation and variability.
status: Defect models and materials improvements are substantial; a universal predictive microscopic account is lacking.
why: Enables targeted manufacturing fixes rather than empirical process iteration.
key_works: Nathalie de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.

title: Reproducible low-loss superconducting interfaces at scale
open: Achieve wafer- and batch-level control of interface loss with predictive relationships among processing, defect populations, coherence, and fabrication yield.
status: High-coherence individual devices do not establish a scalable distribution of device quality.
why: Large processors are limited by weak devices and correlated process failures.
key_works: de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.

title: Nonequilibrium quasiparticle control under active operation
open: Predict and suppress quasiparticle generation and transport during realistic readout, reset, control, and radiation exposure without introducing compensating noise.
status: Quasiparticle mitigation and burst observations identify mechanisms, but complete operational control remains unresolved.
why: Quasiparticles can produce both local relaxation and correlated failures.
key_works: McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219; Philip Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*.

title: Parallel high-fidelity fluxonium gates in dense processors
open: Preserve favorable fluxonium gate performance under simultaneous operation, frequency crowding, spectator coupling, fabrication spread, and repeated error-correction cycles.
status: Coupler and small-system gate advances are partial results; isolated-pair fidelity does not establish dense-array behavior.
why: Tests whether fluxonium’s coherence advantages survive processor integration.
key_works: Guinn et al. (2024), *Tunable inductive coupler for high-fidelity gates between fluxonium qubits*, DOI:10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.020326; *CNOT gates in inductively coupled multi-fluxonium systems*, arXiv:2512.11756.

title: Cryogenic wiring without prohibitive heat load
open: Scale control and readout connections while keeping conductive heat, microwave dissipation, thermalization, crosstalk, and maintenance within a complete refrigerator budget.
status: Engineering studies for hundred-qubit systems establish useful baselines; extrapolation by adding independent lines is not sustainable indefinitely.
why: Physical wiring can become the scaling wall before qubit fabrication.
key_works: Simon Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*, arXiv:1806.07862.

title: Cryogenic control electronics with full noise accounting
open: Integrate low-temperature controllers that reduce system cost and wiring without degrading qubits through power dissipation, phase noise, electromagnetic interference, or shared-control faults.
status: Component demonstrations do not establish a favorable complete-system tradeoff.
why: Moves classical control closer to the processor without making the refrigerator or noise environment worse.
key_works: Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*; Marco Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.

title: Fast multiplexed readout with bounded correlated error
open: Increase simultaneous readout throughput while jointly controlling assignment error, measurement-induced transitions, resonator collisions, and backaction on unmeasured qubits.
status: Fast and multiplexed readout exist; their joint scalable error model remains a system-level challenge.
why: Syndrome extraction repeatedly exercises the readout system, making small correlations consequential.
key_works: Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.

title: Adaptive calibration that improves logical reliability
open: Show that online parameter tracking and recalibration reduce logical failures after accounting for calibration interruptions, estimator mistakes, and feedback-induced instability.
status: Real-time tracking of fluctuating relaxation rates is advancing; improved physical estimates do not automatically imply better logical operation.
why: Large processors cannot rely on a permanently stationary calibration.
key_works: F. Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, DOI:10.1103/gk1b-stl3.

title: High-throughput shuttling through large ion-trap networks
open: Route ions through many junctions with bounded heating, loss, timing variation, and congestion while supporting continuous parallel computation.
status: Quantum-CCD and racetrack architectures demonstrate essential primitives, not arbitrary-scale transport reliability.
why: Converts long-lived isolated qubits into a scalable connected processor.
key_works: J. M. Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; S. A. Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828.

title: Microscopic origin of anomalous ion-trap heating
open: Identify dominant microscopic electric-field-noise mechanisms across relevant surfaces and temperatures, with predictions that survive changes in fabrication and cleaning.
status: Decades of measurements constrain models, but no single predictive microscopic explanation covers the full experimental landscape.
why: Heating limits miniaturization, transport, and motional gates.
key_works: Michael Brownnutt, Markus Kumph, Peter Rabl, and Rainer Blatt (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*, arXiv:1409.6572.

title: Integrated optical delivery for many ion zones
open: Deliver individually controlled, phase-stable optical fields to many zones with manageable optical power, alignment, fabrication variation, and crosstalk.
status: Integrated and broadcast control approaches are partial solutions; complete large-network optical control remains a scaling challenge.
why: Free-space optical complexity can overwhelm the benefits of integrated traps.
key_works: Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828.

title: Parallel entangling gates with shared motional resources
open: Execute many simultaneous entangling gates while suppressing spectator excitation, mode crowding, transport-induced changes, and correlated gate errors.
status: High-fidelity individual gates do not settle dense simultaneous operation.
why: Parallel throughput determines whether long coherence translates into fast computation.
key_works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*.

title: Cooling during computation without damaging stored information
open: Integrate sympathetic cooling, transport, and repeated gates so that motional entropy is removed without unacceptable memory, scattering, or species-crosstalk errors.
status: Cooling primitives exist; sustained many-zone scheduling with a complete logical error budget remains an integration problem.
why: Transport and gates continually replenish the motion that must be removed.
key_works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Brownnutt et al. (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*.

title: Networked ion gates competitive with local fault tolerance
open: Raise remote entangling-gate fidelity and throughput enough that modular ion computation beats simply enlarging or reconfiguring a local processor.
status: Distributed computation across an optical link is demonstrated; a remote gate’s existence is not the remaining problem.
why: Determines whether photonic modularity is a performance advantage rather than a connectivity demonstration.
key_works: D. Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*, arXiv:2407.00835.

title: Continuous loading during error-corrected computation
open: Replenish lost atoms while executing repeated syndrome extraction and logical gates, without disturbing stored information or invalidating calibration.
status: Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system was reported in 2025; continuous replenishment plus full error-corrected computation is a stronger target.
why: Atom loss must become a recoverable service event rather than a run-ending failure.
key_works: Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660.

title: Complete logical recovery from atom loss
open: Detect loss, replace or reroute the missing carrier, restore the code, and continue computation with a quantified logical failure probability.
status: Erasure conversion and reconfigurable logical processors provide ingredients; the full recovery cost depends on when and where loss occurs.
why: Converts a dominant physical failure into manageable logical maintenance.
key_works: Wu et al. (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540; Dolev Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*.

title: Correlation-aware benchmarking of parallel Rydberg gates
open: Characterize and suppress correlated errors during large simultaneous gate layers, including common laser noise, blockade imperfections, and spatial intensity variation.
status: High-fidelity parallel entangling gates are demonstrated; aggregate fidelity does not fully specify the correlations relevant to error correction.
why: Common-mode gate errors can dominate logical performance.
key_works: Simon J. Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420.

title: Motional robustness of repeated neutral-atom gates
open: Maintain gate performance through repeated excitation, transport, heating, and recooling, with a model connecting motional state to logical error.
status: Strong individual and parallel gate results do not establish arbitrarily long sequences under evolving motion.
why: Internal-state coherence alone does not capture the full atom’s computational behavior.
key_works: Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420.

title: Mid-circuit atom readout without spectator damage
open: Repeatedly measure selected atoms while preserving neighboring data qubits and maintaining an error model suitable for fault-tolerant decoding.
status: Logical-processor demonstrations supply partial evidence; repeated large-scale selective readout remains a demanding combined optical and architectural problem.
why: Error correction requires frequent measurement without globally resetting the machine.
